quote: Oh, I just I'm with the design team. I help, like, get you their design going so we can find out what we can offer you.
stewart_read: The rep never gives a clean company/role statement matching the script template; instead he improvises after the customer references a quote already sent, leaving the customer's confusion about who is calling unresolved.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may have judged that clarifying could re-open a longer conversation and chose brevity to move to verify faster — but there's no evidence of this being deliberate; it reads as an unprepared reaction to an unexpected customer opener.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to have a one-line legitimacy statement ready for the common case of 'you already sent me something' — acknowledge the prior touch, then re-state who they are and why they're calling now.

quote: Black Hills. Those are some of the questions on your fucking questionnaire.
stewart_read: This is an overt frustration signal, not a vulnerability disclosure, but the same principle applies: it's a trust-and-tone gift that tells the rep the customer feels re-interrogated. The rep does not acknowledge the frustration at all and moves straight to the next verify item.
coaching_implication: When a customer swears at the pace/redundancy of questions, the rep should briefly acknowledge ('I know, just a couple more and we're done') rather than pushing through silently — this is a repair moment the rep skipped.

stewart_read: The customer gives a clear, specific bill figure. The rep's only response is a flat repeat-back with no emotional flip or acknowledgment of pain.
coaching_implication: This is a missed anchor-and-flip moment; coach the rep to tie the number to utility-vs-solar framing even briefly before moving to the next question.

quote: I don't want it mounted on my roof. I got five acres. I like it mounted on the ground.
stewart_read: Five acres and an explicit preference for a larger, ground-mounted system signals a highly qualified, high-usage property that would be attractive to install if Ion offered ground mount — this is valuable intel even though it results in a DQ here.
coaching_implication: Even on a DQ call, this detail (large property, owner actively wants solar, just wrong format) is worth logging for any future ground-mount offering or referral opportunity — the rep let it pass with no notation beyond the immediate no.

quote: Okay. We only do roofs and many like, residential roofs for the home. We can't do ground mounts.
stewart_read: The rep correctly identifies that Ion cannot serve a ground-mount request, but delivers it as a flat capability wall with no exploration of alternatives (e.g., is there also a roof on the property that could be used, or any other structure) before letting the customer disengage.
alternative_hypothesis: This could be read as appropriately fast triage on a hard DQ, since ground mount truly isn't offered — but the schema's dq_rules list does not currently enumerate a ground-mount-only condition as a hard disqualifier, so this scenario has no existing script or rule to follow. That gap, not a rep persuasion failure, is the primary issue.
coaching_implication: Flag to Kenny that ground_mount_only_no_roof_option is not currently in dq_rules and should be added as an explicit hard DQ with a scripted response, since reps are currently handling it ad hoc.

quote: Oh, I didn't I'm not interested.
stewart_read: The call ends immediately on the DQ with no attempt to check whether the customer has a roof on any structure, no cross-sell mention (e.g., in-house roofing team, if relevant), and no button-up of any kind — this is a valid DQ but the exit itself has zero procedure.
alternative_hypothesis: Given this is a legitimate hard DQ (Ion cannot serve the ask), there may be nothing left to button up — a graceful, quick close may be the correct move rather than a failure to anchor a next step.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep on a brief, warm sign-off even on DQs ('Appreciate you telling me that up front, wish we could help with the ground mount') rather than the bare 'Thanks. Have a great day.'
